evidence.text: Origin unclear. Variously explained as a pictograph of a snake, a vulva, a funnel, a crying child, or an ideograph depicting a pause in speech.
女陰也。象形。

Pictogram (象形) — A child (子) with their mouth (口) open crying. The original form of 嗁 (OC *l'eː, “to cry”) (Chi Hsu-Sheng, 2014). The child's arms were removed during bronze inscriptions and the two components fused together in the modern form.
Other various possible explanations include:
* The traditional glyph origin given in Shuowen explains the character to be a pictogram (象形) of female genitalia.
* It was once interchangeable with 它 and may have originated as a simplification. Hence, it could be the pictogram of a snake.
* It may have been created to represent the modal particle (語氣詞／语气词 (yǔqìcí)). In some bronze inscriptions, it appears to be a mouth (口) with a curved line descending from it to represent air coming out of the mouth.
* It is possibly a pictogram (象形) of an ancient funnel or wash basin. It may be an early form of 匜.
* It may have signified a big-headed scorpion with its legs flattened, signifying as something very "flat" or "stretched out".
; classical sentence-ending copulative particle, topic particle
Unclear. Possibly Sino-Tibetan, connectable to Tibetan ལ (la), which is often used as a marker (for oblique locative, dative, possessor in constructions with a copula verb, etc.) but also a topicalizer like ནི (ni, “as for”) (Schuessler, 2007).
On the other hand, Pulleyblank (1995) notes the similarity with anteclassical 唯 (OC *ɢʷi) as a copula and a topicalizer.
; also, too, as well
女陰也。象形。
also; classical final particle of strong affirmation or identity

evidence.text: The Han-dynasty dictionary gives 女陰也。象形 (“female genitalia; pictograph”). This is an ancient lexicographic interpretation, not independent confirmation of the depicted referent.

evidence.field: paleographic analysis, as reported in search result
evidence.text: The result reports one scholarly analysis that 也 depicts a child with an open mouth crying, is the original graph for 啼 ‘cry’, and was clearly distinct from 它 in early scripts; it says the two began to be confused only after Emperor Wu of Han. This is a reported scholarly analysis, not independently verified from the article text in this session.
evidence.title: 劉洪濤：上古音“也”字歸部簡論

evidence.source: Zhang Zhenlin, “先秦古文字材料中的語氣詞,” Chinese University of Hong Kong PDF
evidence.field: survey of pre-Qin excavated evidence for particles
evidence.text: The article says no simple modal particles are attested in oracle-bone inscriptions or Shang bronze inscriptions in its survey, and reports earlier scholarship arguing that 也, 邪, 矣, and 焉 are absent from oracle-bone and bronze texts. It cautions that transmitted Book of Songs and Book of Documents examples are difficult to date and may have undergone copying or alteration. Thus a particle use cannot be securely dated from a generalized gloss list, and these observations leave the precise earliest attestation unsettled.
evidence.title: 先秦古文字材料中的語氣詞

evidence.source: Marco Caboara, HKUST Research Portal, peer-reviewed chapter record
evidence.text: The chapter proposes a grammaticalization path from focus particle to copula for 也 and analyzes its functions and copular use in the Guodian manuscript corpus. This is a grammatical account of the word’s uses, not evidence for the graph’s depicted origin. The repository record dates the chapter to January 2016, pages 447–460.
evidence.title: From Discourse to Grammar, But Not All the Way: Grammaticalization and Redundancy of the Classical Chinese Function Word ye 也 in Pre-Qin Texts, with Special Attention to the Guodian Bamboo Manuscripts

evidence.text: The entry presents Spring and Autumn, Warring States, bronze, Chu manuscript, small-seal, and Shuowen forms, but says the form references are mostly derived from Richard Sears’ Chinese Etymology site and collections including Jinwen Bian and Yinxu Jiaguwen Bian. It lists the crying-child proposal and alternatives including the Shuowen genitalia account, possible confusion with snake graph 它, a mouth-and-air interpretation, and a vessel/funnel proposal related to 匜. These are competing hypotheses; this page does not settle the original referent. No glyph image was visually inspected for this report.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: No primary oracle-bone or bronze inscription image, catalog entry, or paleographic dictionary page was successfully inspected; the local glyph-file leads remain unverified and were not visually inspected.

The original referent of 也 remains disputed among the Shuowen genitalia interpretation, the child-crying analysis, and vessel, snake, or mouth-related proposals. Available external material does not establish the winning account or prove graphic corruption.

The exact earliest securely dated occurrence of the graph and the earliest securely dated use of 也 as a particle were not established. A scholarly survey reports no simple particles in oracle-bone or Shang bronze evidence and warns that transmitted classics can be chronologically unstable; claims of an early usage should be tied to a particular dated artifact or manuscript.
The proposed relation of 也 as the original graph for 啼 is reported through a secondary page and a search-result abstract; the original paleographic argument and inscriptions were not inspected.

No meaningful graphic component decomposition is independently supported, so no component semantic or phonetic roles are assigned. There is no proposed sound component requiring component-versus-host reading comparison.

Unicode Unihan official record for U+4E5F was attempted but could not be opened. The provided local kMandarin yě and Baxter–Sagart MC yaeX, OC *lAjʔ rows are preserved as local evidence only; their click-through source verification is incomplete.

Later sense history from sentence-final/assertive or focus particle to copular-like uses and modern ‘also’ was not established chronologically. The searched sources support grammatical analyses, not a dated semantic chain; no chronology is inferred from dictionary gloss order.
The proposed Sino-Tibetan comparison and comparison with 唯 remain hypotheses noted by Wiktionary; their primary arguments and sound correspondences were not checked.

The ancient referent remains disputed: Shuowen’s genitalia interpretation conflicts with Academia Sinica’s snake interpretation; the child-crying and vessel/funnel proposals were not independently verified from their underlying paleographic arguments.

No primary inscription image or catalog entry was inspected directly. The Sinica page provides a bronze catalog reference 集成10008 and labels later forms, but does not supply an inspected inscription photograph in the accessible text.

Exact earliest attested graph and exact earliest securely dated particle use were not established. A Fudan research summary points to excavated Chu manuscripts, but the article could not be opened and manuscript tokens/dates were not checked.

No sequence of particle, copular, affirmative, focus, or ‘also’ senses is demonstrated here. The dictionary lists modern senses and classical functions but does not establish semantic chronology; no chronology is inferred from gloss order.

No component decomposition is supported, so no semantic/phonetic roles are assigned. Whole-graph borrowing for function-word uses is proposed by the Shuowen commentary and Sinica database, but the object/name/pronunciation behind either pictographic account is not independently established.
Unicode Unihan official record for U+4E5F could not be opened. The local yě reading remains locally sourced only. No sound component is proposed, so no comparison reading is applicable.
